title: Galaxy Cluster Abell 2218 - a Cosmic Magnifying Glass
caption: The galaxy cluster Abell 2218, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Abell 2218 · constellation Draco · about z=0.17 (redshift) away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, Andrew Fruchter (STScI), and the ERO team (STScI + ST-ECF)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble picture shows Abell 2218, a massive cluster of galaxies that the source likens to a giant magnifying glass in space. Seen in the direction of Draco, the cluster is some 2 billion light-years from Earth.

The comparison refers to gravitational lensing. A cluster this heavy bends and brightens the light of galaxies that sit far behind it, so objects that would otherwise be too faint to study can be seen. That is why the cluster is cataloged as an example of gravitationally lensed galaxies in the early Universe.

The image has a place in Hubble's own history. It was among the first views the telescope took after the servicing mission of December 1999, when Hubble returned to scanning the sky. A galaxy cluster is a large gathering of galaxies bound by gravity, and the more mass it holds, the more strongly it bends light.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 observed Abell 2218 in visible and near-infrared light through filters at 450, 606 and 814 nm. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The galaxies here are far too faint for the eye, and Hubble's exposures gather light from them that no eyepiece view could show.
